Honestly, after reading all the details, I have to lean toward “yes," you would be the asshole if you started dating your friend’s ex under these circumstances.

Here’s why: GB and HR literally just broke up, and not only do the three of you share the same friend group, but you were also close friends with HR while she dated GB—even having some unspoken romantic feelings for her at the time. Even if you weren’t the cause of their breakup (which you’ve said you weren’t), the optics don’t look great. You only started talking to HR again three weeks ago, found out she and GB broke up, and immediately moved to ask her out. 

Add to that: the friend group hadn’t even processed the breakup because they were “kept in the dark,” so seeing you jump in with HR almost straight away comes across as super insensitive—whether it was your intention or not. Their immediate backlash is honestly pretty understandable given how fast this all happened and how close you all are.

You say you’re not seeking drama and believe people should “respect breakups, move on, and not be hostile,” and while I agree with that in theory, respecting a breakup also means giving friendships and the ex (in this case, GB) time to process everything, rather than quickly transitioning into dating her ex as soon as the news breaks—especially in the same friend group.

The fact that you used to have romantic feelings for HR, never acted on them, and were admittedly “not in a state to have a relationship earlier,” makes this timing seem even more suspicious, whether or not that’s fair to you.

TL;DR: with all the context, yes, YWBTBA (you would be the asshole) to start dating GB’s ex, at least for now. If this relationship is meant to be, waiting a little longer out of respect for GB and your friend group will show a lot more maturity and sensitivity.

Honestly, I don't think you would be the asshole if you started dating your friend's ex. Let's lay out the facts: GB and HR broke up, and you, GB, and HR are all in the same friend group. While HR and GB were dating, you became close friends with HR and had some romantic feelings, but you didn’t act on those feelings out of respect. You’ve also made it clear that you were not the cause of their breakup.

Three weeks ago, you started talking to HR and only then learned about the breakup because the group kept it quiet. After this, you asked HR out, she said yes, and when you shared it with some friends, you faced immediate backlash. You say you’re not seeking drama and you believe people should respect breakups, move on, and not be hostile toward new partners.

You’re starting to doubt yourself—understandably, since the group’s reaction can sting—but from what you’ve described, it doesn’t sound like you did anything morally wrong. You waited until the relationship was done, you didn’t influence their breakup, and you weren’t trying to cause drama. Sometimes, people just move on and sometimes new feelings grow—that’s how life works. Respecting breakups isn’t just about not interfering, but also allowing people to move forward and find happiness, even within friend circles.

You even mention that earlier, you didn’t feel okay getting into a relationship, so it’s not like you were pursuing HR the whole time—you were being considerate of yourself and others.

In my opinion, your friend group should be understanding, and it’s unfair for them to be hostile. Adults should be able to handle people moving on. So my answer is no, you would not be the asshole if you started dating HR.

Honestly, I think YWBT if you started dating your friend’s ex in this situation.

Here’s why: GB and HR broke up, and you (the narrator) are clearly still in the same friend group as them both. You mention that while GB and HR were dating, you and HR were close friends, and you had some romantic feelings for HR, even though you never acted on them at the time. Kudos for not acting unethically then, but that history can definitely make things look like you’ve been waiting for your shot—and that makes it tricky.

You didn’t cause the breakup, and I can tell you tried to keep it above board. Still, you only found out about their breakup three weeks ago (since the friend group was kept in the dark), and you almost immediately started talking to HR and asked her out as soon as you found out she was single. From the outside, this is super fast, especially since everyone in your group still sees HR as “GB’s ex”. The backlash you're getting makes sense because, to your friends, it looks opportunistic—and no matter what you say, people are going to speculate you had “ulterior motives” while HR and GB were still together.

Bottom line: Once you involve romance with a friend’s ex—especially in a small tight friend group and so soon after the breakup—you risk hurting feelings and fracturing those friendships. Especially since there’s an additional layer with you and HR being extra close before and already having feelings. Sometimes just because you “can” doesn’t mean you “should,” at least not without giving much more time and maybe even talking to GB first.

So yeah, in this specific case, YWBT if you go ahead and date HR right now. Maybe cool off for a bit and revisit when (or if) your group moves on!

Honestly, I don't think I'd be the asshole if I started dating my friend's ex in this situation.

Here’s why: GB and HR broke up without telling our friend group, so it wasn’t exactly clear where everyone stood. While GB and HR were together, HR and I were close friends and, yeah, I had some feelings, but I totally respected their relationship and never acted on anything. For everyone’s peace of mind, I wasn’t at all the reason they broke up.

Three weeks ago, I caught up with HR and found out she and GB weren’t a thing anymore. Since all of us in the friend group had been kept in the dark about the breakup, I couldn’t have known what was going on until HR told me herself. After talking for a while, I asked her out, and she said yes—which seemed totally fine to both of us.

When I let some friends know about us, the backlash was wild. People accused me of being awful and said I was just trying to cause drama, but that’s just not true. I respect both GB and HR, and if either of them had issues they wanted to discuss, I’m open to it, but at the end of the day, what happened felt natural and no one was betrayed. 

With all the facts considered, I know I’m not the bad guy here just for asking someone out after a breakup I wasn’t even aware of at the time it happened. So, no, I wouldn’t be the asshole.

GB and HR recently broke up, and though you, GB, and HR are all in the same friend group, the breakup was kept secret from everyone. Even if you didn’t intend any harm, it seems disrespectful to your friend and inconsiderate of the group dynamic to move so quickly and keep everyone in the dark. I think waiting, being more open about your intentions, or at least talking honestly with your friends first would have saved a lot of backlash.

Honestly, I don’t think you would be the asshole for dating your friend’s ex in this situation. GB and HR have already broken up, which is important. Also, it’s not like you were trying to make things dramatic—the reality is your entire friend group, including you, was kept in the dark about the breakup. I understand it can feel weird in a close-knit friend group, but you’re both adults who are free to make your own choices. In my opinion, you’re not wrong for following your feelings, and it definitely doesn’t make you a bad person. As long as you’re respectful and considerate, I say go for it.

Honestly, based on everything shared, I do think WIBTA if you started dating your friend's ex. You, GB, and HR are all in the same group of friends, and that makes things a lot more intense. I have to say yes: YWBTA here because of the issues it's already causing and how messy it is for everyone involved. Sometimes feelings aren’t enough reason to go ahead, especially with mutual friends in the mix.

Honestly, I don’t think I’d be the asshole for dating a friend’s ex in this situation. First off, GB and HR broke up, and it was kept totally quiet from our whole friend group, so none of us even knew they weren’t together anymore until much later. When I finally asked HR out (and she said yes!), some people flipped out and called me awful, saying I shouldn’t do it and I just want drama… even though none of that’s true.

Yes, back when HR and GB were dating, HR and I were really close friends, and I can admit I did start to catch some feelings, but I never acted on them while they were together—I fully respected their relationship. Just to clear things up, I had nothing to do with their breakup; that was entirely between them, and I wasn’t even remotely involved. 

I know some in the group think this would cause drama or I’m doing this for attention, but that’s honestly not true. I tried to be as honest and discreet as possible once things with HR changed, and wouldn’t be doing this if I thought it would hurt my friends. At the end of the day, nobody “owns” someone after a breakup, especially when the relationship is over and both parties move on. 

So yeah, I really don’t think I’d be the asshole here. As long as everything happened after the breakup with zero overlap, and I wasn’t sneaking around or causing trouble—why shouldn’t two people see where things go? I stand by my decision.

Reading everyone else’s takes, I can see why a lot of people feel strongly that jumping into dating HR right after her breakup with GB (especially when it was kept secret from the whole friend group) would make me the asshole. I get their point that the timing looks bad and could feel like a betrayal to some, considering the history and how tight-knit we all are. It’s true that moving forward so soon caught everyone off-guard, and if the tables were turned, even with zero overlap or ill intent, it might sting to see two close friends pair off out of nowhere. But with all that in mind, I still lean toward my original view: I wouldn’t be the asshole here, because I didn’t pursue anything until after learning—directly from HR—that they had broken up, and there was never any sneaking around or sabotage. That said, I definitely underestimated how much people’s perceptions and group dynamics factor in—and maybe I should’ve checked in with GB and handled introducing the new relationship with the group more sensitively. I don’t agree that I’ve done something outright wrong or malicious, but I am willing to admit the timing could have been better thought out, and I’ll try to be more considerate if navigating things like this again. So, still no, but I recognize the need for care in handling everyone’s feelings moving forward.

After considering everyone’s perspectives, I still largely stand by my previous view, though I can see more shades of grey now. While a few people made compelling points about not “owning” exes and how it isn’t wrong to move on—as long as things were above board—I still think the way everything unfolded here makes it understandable that friends would be upset. The immediate shift from not knowing GB and HR had broken up to you asking HR out, and sharing it with the group, naturally looks thoughtless (even if your intent was otherwise). The shared history and your old feelings for HR might look like you were waiting for your chance, and, to be honest, appearances matter in a close friend group. That said, I think my view isn’t quite as black-and-white now; your intentions seem sincere and you didn’t cross any obvious lines, but the timing and lack of communication made things much messier than necessary. So for now, I would still say yes, YWBT if you started dating HR right away—with all the tension and hurt it’s clearly causing in your group, letting things settle would probably be the best move. However, with more openness or time, this could change; it’s just that right now, it’s too soon for comfort.

After reading through everyone’s perspectives, I still lean toward thinking WIBTA—though I understand a bit more where the other side is coming from. Multiple people point out that you waited until HR and GB were genuinely broken up and that you took HR’s feelings into account—and I respect that you didn’t pursue anything while HR was still with GB. But on the other hand, other commenters echo my concerns about group dynamics: the fact that the breakup was kept secret, and how quickly things transitioned once you found out feels like an emotional minefield, especially since everyone in the friend group hadn’t even processed the breakup. Looking at the reactions, the potential for hurt and drama really is huge, even if your motives weren’t shady. I haven’t changed my position entirely, but I recognize there’s an honest side of “life moves on” here that I can appreciate—even though I think, considering the shock in your group and how raw things probably still are, going forward so fast would still be the wrong move. My opinion: you would be the asshole if you went ahead without giving things more time, open conversations, and space for everyone (including GB and your other friends) to process. But I get that others see it differently, and as circumstances settle, my answer might eventually change.

After reading everyone’s perspectives, I still mostly stand by my original view that I wouldn’t be the asshole for dating a friend’s ex in this particular circumstance—but I definitely see why people feel otherwise, and it’s making me question if I underestimated the emotional impact. So, I still feel I’m not the asshole for starting to date HR after the breakup once I had the facts, but I do want to be sensitive to how others perceive it and maybe should have communicated more carefully with the group and with GB in particular.

So, my view is mostly the same, but I’m more sympathetic to both sides; still, for now, I think it’s better to wait.

After really taking in everyone's perspectives, I’m a bit more torn than before, but my core opinion hasn’t shifted much—though I now recognize even more why there’s tension. Overall, I still don’t think starting to date HR automatically makes you the bad guy, but now I think you’d be wise to address people’s hurts, given how messy it got so fast.

After reading everyone’s perspectives and reflecting more, I still lean toward thinking “yes, you would be the asshole—at least a bit—if you started dating your friend’s ex in this situation, though I’m less absolute about it than I was before. I get where those saying 'you’re not wrong and it’s nobody’s business' are coming from: you didn’t interfere with the relationship when HR and GB were together, and you waited until they’d broken up (even if the breakup wasn’t public right away). So, while I personally stand by my answer that you would, to some degree, be the asshole, I can see how your intent wasn’t malicious and why some disagree. If you go forward, at least be as transparent and compassionate as possible with everyone involved.

After really considering everyone’s perspectives, I can see why there’s such a strong reaction. After considering all the new comments and taking a step back, my view hasn’t changed drastically, but I definitely have a better grasp of just how much the timing and group dynamics matter in this situation. The majority seem to agree that my intentions weren’t malicious—I didn’t make a move until after HR and GB had already broken up, and there was never any shady behavior. I still don’t see myself as the asshole for being honest about my feelings and not interfering in the previous relationship, but I have to acknowledge more fully now that the upset in the group was inevitable given the circumstances and that starting to date HR so soon, without giving others (and especially GB) more time or having direct conversations first, definitely made things harder on everyone. So, while my core stance stands—I'm not the asshole for wanting to move forward with HR—I’m also not ignoring the legitimate hurt feelings, and I see that slowing down to respect everyone’s emotional space would have gone a long way. Going forward, I’ll be a lot more mindful and open with the group—not out of guilt, but out of respect for how messy these situations really can be.

Reading through all the responses again makes me even more aware of just how much the timing and communication matter as much as the actual facts in a situation like this. There are strong arguments that as long as I waited until after HR and GB’s breakup—and didn’t pursue anything while they were together—I’m not technically in the wrong, and adults don’t own their exes. While my core opinion is still that it was premature (so, YWBT, at least in this specific context), I’m more empathetic now to the arguments on both sides, and I recognize that with more honest communication and a little time, it probably wouldn’t be nearly as much of an issue. In sum: I wouldn't label it a black-and-white “asshole” move, but going ahead right now would be careless to the group’s dynamics and GB’s feelings, so pausing and opening up more seems like the right call.

After weighing everyone’s arguments and reflecting some more, I’m still leaning toward “yes, you would be the asshole if you jumped right into dating HR now,” but I’ll admit my position isn’t as rigid as before. The points about respecting someone’s autonomy and not “owning” exes are valid, and I recognize you waited until after HR and GB had split—no overlap, no outright betrayal. Still, between the secrecy around the breakup, your quick pivot to starting things with HR, and how it blindsided the whole friend group, I think the social and emotional fallout can’t be dismissed. Several people articulated that even if all the facts were technically above board, feelings matter, especially in a tight circle—optics and group trust got rattled, even if your intent wasn’t bad. I’m not saying you’re malicious, and, given time, this could be seen in a much kinder light, but for now I still think moving forward so quickly after learning about the split—before anyone had a chance to process—would make you at least a minor asshole in the eyes of your group. The best move, in my view, is still to hold back, be transparent with everyone (especially GB), and give things breathing room. That would help minimize hurt and show respect for everyone’s feelings, and maybe in doing so, shift even my own opinion moving forward.

Reflecting on everyone’s feedback, my core position that I wouldn’t strictly be the asshole for starting to date HR after her breakup with GB hasn’t radically changed, but I do feel less certain and more mindful of the group dynamic than before. It’s become really clear that, even without malicious intent or overlap, the timing feels abrupt and blindsided the friend group, especially since my old feelings for HR might look suspicious regardless of when anything started. I still think that, in terms of intention and principle, I acted respectfully—waiting for a breakup before doing anything and not hiding how I felt but only after the relationship ended. At the same time, I now see that I poorly managed the optics, and I undervalued both the need for transparency (especially with GB) and how group cohesion relies on trust and sensitive timing. There’s a part of me that feels frustrated to be viewed negatively for something genuine, but I respect that others are hurting and that my choices played a role in this. In sum, I still don’t feel like an outright asshole for dating HR (since adults can move on), but I’ll freely admit I could and should have slowed down, communicated more, and been more thoughtful toward everyone in the friend group. So while my core answer is mostly the same—no, I’m not TA for dating her—I now think the way I handled things made hurts that I could’ve avoided, and I do want to do better by everyone moving forward.

Reading through everyone else’s thoughtful arguments makes me more empathetic to both sides, but ultimately I still feel that, right now, you would be the asshole if you started dating HR so soon after her secret breakup with GB. The points others made—especially about there being no actual cheating or intentional harm, and adults having every right to move on—made me realize it’s not so black-and-white, and I do get why some people see nothing wrong given you waited for a clean break. But for me, the unique context of a very close group, your pre-existing feelings, and how the news hit everyone all at once is still reason enough to press pause; emotional fallout and messy perceptions matter in friendships, not just technicalities. I recognize your honesty and the lack of clear-cut rule-breaking, and maybe with more time or some open conversations this wouldn’t be such a big deal, but right now, I think waiting before making things official with HR is the best way to respect everyone’s feelings and hopefully keep your core friendships intact.

Having read the latest wave of replies and really considered everyone’s input, I can honestly say I feel even more the weight of group dynamics and the overall optics than I did at first. I now see that waiting a bit, or at least some open conversations with GB and maybe the group, is crucial—not only for appearances, but out of basic respect and care for the people involved. In summary, no, you’re not simply the asshole for starting to date HR, but given the circumstances, you’d be wise to press pause and handle it with more sensitivity if you want to keep your friendships healthy.

Having listened carefully to everyone’s recent thoughts and reflected on the responses again, I still lean toward “yes, you would be at least a bit the asshole if you moved forward with dating HR right now,” though my stance has softened further, and I appreciate the nuances more. However, I more clearly see how the line between right and wrong here isn’t absolute, and the weight of your choices hinges on both ethics and empathy. If it were me, I still think the most respectful path would’ve been to hold off, check in with GB, and let the group catch up emotionally, but I also acknowledge that adults don’t need to ask for permission to pursue mutual feelings once a relationship’s truly over. So, my updated take: right now, given the abruptness and the circumstances, you would still be (at least a little) the asshole to push ahead—but as time passes, feelings settle, and conversations happen, I could see that changing. I definitely urge handling things delicately and with extra transparency. Overall, my view has softened and I’m more open to seeing this differently over time, but, currently, I’d answer WIBTA with a cautious “yes,” mainly because of the hurt and shock still rippling through your group.
